_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Programmes such as inclusive schooling, teacher training, assistive devices and community-based rehabilitation help children with disabilities in poorer countries get into school and learn more. Putting children in mainstream classrooms with support works better than separate special schools. The evidence for this is reasonably solid.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: An education ministry official or donor programme officer (for example at a bilateral aid agency, UNICEF or the Global Partnership for Education) deciding which disability-inclusive education interventions to fund or scale. The choices include teacher training, assistive technology, inclusive versus special schooling, cash transfers and community-based programmes.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: The primary evaluations (controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies in low- and middle-income countries) consistently show meaningful gains in enrolment, attendance and learning for children with disabilities. The same programme types come out on top across settings and impairment types, and systematic reviews rate this evidence as moderate or high certainty. That would simply confirm the common belief.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Evaluated interventions in low- and middle-income countries that aim to improve educational outcomes for children and young people with disabilities. Outcomes are enrolment, attendance, retention, completion, learning, and participation or inclusion in school. The page covers whether such interventions work overall and how their effects compare by intervention type, impairment type and setting.

out.what: Effectiveness of disability-inclusive education in high-income countries
out.why: Different school systems, resources and evidence base; the question is restricted to low- and middle-income countries.

out.what: Health, rehabilitation or functional outcomes not tied to education
out.why: The question concerns educational outcomes; clinical effectiveness of therapies is a separate literature.

out.what: How many children with disabilities are out of school, and why
out.why: That is about prevalence and barriers, not about whether programmes work.

out.what: Whether inclusive education is a legal or human-rights obligation (e.g., under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, CRPD)
out.why: A normative and legal question that evidence on effectiveness cannot settle.

out.what: General education interventions not targeted at, or not reporting outcomes for, children with disabilities
out.why: Effects for the general pupil population cannot be assumed to hold for this group.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Effect sizes and outcome data from randomised and quasi-experimental evaluations in low- and middle-income countries. These include changes in enrolment, attendance, dropout and completion rates, test scores or learning assessments, and validated measures of participation for children with disabilities against a comparison group. Sample sizes, follow-up length and attrition are reported alongside.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty or confidence ratings given by systematic reviews or evidence panels (for example GRADE ratings in Campbell or 3ie reviews, or risk-of-bias judgements) on whether the body of evidence supports an effect for each intervention type. This includes reviewers' explicit judgements that evidence is insufficient or too heterogeneous to rank interventions.
